title: Scattered-Mind Recitation: Answers to a Visitor's Questions
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Single-mindedness — this is the key to correct study and practice in the Pure Land school.

inline.s: Single-mindedness — this is the key to correct study and practice in the Pure Land school.
Master Shandao, an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, taught:
Reciting sutras, contemplating, recollecting, bowing to the Buddha, reciting the Buddha's name, and praising and making offerings —
only when done single-mindedly is it proper practice.
Single-minded recitation accords with Amitabha Buddha's vow,
whereas scattered-mind recitation goes against Amitabha Buddha's vow.
The very situation of "scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows"
simply does not exist; it is a false proposition.
Therefore, "if one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation can also bring rebirth" is utterly fallacious.
Master Hanshan pointed it out with piercing directness:
"Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered
(scattered-mind recitation)
, though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain."

Questioner: I have read online an article, "An Analysis of Whether Scattered-Mind Recitation Can Bring Rebirth," and find it specious. Wishing to understand exactly where it errs, I raise the following questions and ask you to answer them.
Question: The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says:
"From the contemplation of the sun down through the thirteenth contemplation is called concentrated good; the three kinds of merit and the nine grades are called scattered good."
Does this not show that name-recitation is scattered good, which is to say scattered-mind recitation? Is this so?
Answer:
Master Shandao says that name-recitation is scattered good, but by no means does he say that name-recitation is scattered-mind recitation.
The "scattered" of scattered good is spoken in contrast to the first thirteen contemplations of the Contemplation Sutra (see
the Annotation on the Buddha-Spoken Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life
), which are sustained, focused, and subtle states of samādhi. The "scattered" of scattered-mind recitation, by contrast, means wandering in wild thoughts while reciting.
[The "concentration" spoken of as the sustained, focused, and subtle samādhi of the first thirteen contemplations in the Contemplation Sutra]
Among these thirteen contemplations, the most elementary is the contemplation of the sun. In the Contemplation Sutra the Buddha says:

"One should arouse the thought and, sitting upright facing west, intently contemplate the place where the sun is about to set, making the mind firm and stable, focusing the thought without shifting. One sees the sun about to set, shaped like a suspended drum. When the sun has been seen, whether the eyes are closed or open, all should be clearly seen. This is the contemplation of the sun, and it is called the first contemplation."
Concerning this most elementary contemplation of the sun, the World-Honored One taught:
"When the sun has been seen, whether the eyes are closed or open, all should be clearly seen."

(Translation: after seeing the setting sun in contemplation, whether the eyes are closed or open, one must contemplate it perfectly clearly.) See what a subtle state of samādhi this is! How much more so the remaining twelve contemplations. That is why Master Shandao calls these thirteen contemplations concentrated good, and name-recitation, by comparison, scattered good. Therefore the "scattered" of scattered good is by no means the "scattered" of scattered-mind recitation
Moreover, it is in
the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra itself that Master Shandao teaches how one should recite the Buddha's name:
one must recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly.
Master Shandao says:
With a single mind,
single-heartedly recite the name of Amitabha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration, never abandoning it thought after thought
(every thought is the Buddha's name with no wandering thoughts, that is, thought after thought in unbroken succession)
— such a one is named the karma of right concentration,
for it accords with that Buddha's vow
How can one distort "scattered good" into scattered-mind recitation, and then claim that Master Shandao taught scattered-mind recitation?

[Right concentration] Correct samādhi. When body and mind are pure and free from scatteredness, it is called "right concentration." [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind. [For it accords with that Buddha's vow] "With a single mind, single-heartedly recite the name of Amitabha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration, never abandoning it thought after thought" — this is because it accords with Amitabha Buddha's vow.
Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha, and his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha. From this we know that when sentient beings
recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, never abandoning it thought after thought,
this accords with the Buddha's
(Amitabha Buddha's)
vow. Then
scattered-mind recitation goes against the Buddha's
(Amitabha Buddha's)
vow!

What is called "never abandoning it thought after thought" means that every single thought is the name of Amitabha and free of wandering thoughts (if there is a wandering thought, then in that thought the Buddha's name has already been abandoned); this is
single-minded recitation
. Scattered-mind recitation, however, means wandering in wild thoughts while reciting.
Therefore, scattered good is by no means scattered-mind recitation.
As to how one should practise name-recitation, Master Shandao teaches explicitly:
Name-recitation must be an unbroken succession of thoughts; unbroken succession brings rebirth.
Master Shandao says:

"Question: Why do you not have people practise contemplation, but instead simply bid them solely invoke the name? Answer: Because sentient beings' obstacles are heavy, the object is subtle and the mind is coarse, the consciousness is restless and the spirit flies about, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

in compassion bids them solely invoke the name. Precisely because invoking the name is easy, unbroken succession brings rebirth. If one can keep the thoughts unbroken, making this the aim for the whole of one's life
(one who practises in this way to the end of life)
, then ten of ten are reborn and a hundred of a hundred."
(From "The Two Practices of Pure Karma: Exclusive and Mixed"
see
the Pure Land Teachings of Master Shandao

In this passage Master Shandao says: sentient beings' obstacles are heavy, the object is subtle and the mind is coarse, the consciousness is restless and the spirit flies about, and so contemplative recitation (from the contemplation of the sun down through the thirteenth contemplation) is hard to accomplish. Therefore Śākyamuni Buddha teaches name-recitation alone ("solely invoking the name"). Then how should one practise name-recitation? Master Shandao teaches:
"Unbroken succession brings rebirth. If one can keep the thoughts unbroken, making this the aim for the whole of one's life
(one who practises in this way to the end of life)
, then ten of ten are reborn and a hundred of a hundred."
The "unbroken succession of thoughts" spoken of here is single-minded recitation; with scattered-mind recitation, however, the thought of reciting is constantly interrupted by wandering thoughts,
and so it is not an unbroken succession of thoughts. Therefore
scattered-mind recitation utterly contravenes the teaching on name-recitation given by Master Shandao, an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha
— how then can one attain rebirth?
Single-mindedness
(not a scattered mind)
— this is the key to correct study and practice in the Pure Land school.

In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao teaches: reciting sutras, contemplating, recollecting, bowing to the Buddha, reciting the Buddha's name, and praising and making offerings —
all must be done single-mindedly to be proper practice
. Master Shandao says:

"Practice, however, is of two kinds: the first is proper practice, and the second is mixed practice. As for proper practice, one who relies solely upon the practices given in the rebirth sutras is called a practitioner of proper practice. What does that mean?
With a single mind,
single-heartedly read and recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Immeasurable Life Sutra, and the like;
with single-minded focus
contemplate, observe, and recollect the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If one bows, then
with a single mind
single-heartedly bow to that Buddha; if one recites aloud, then
with a single mind
single-heartedly call upon that Buddha; if one praises and offers, then
with a single mind
single-heartedly praise and offer.
This is called proper practice
Question: There is a saying:
"If one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth as well."
Is this saying correct?
Answer: "If one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth as well" —
this is utterly fallacious!
It sunders faith and vows from practice.
Faith, vows, and practice are three interlocking links of one indivisible whole; their relationship is this:
faith awakens vow, vow guides practice; practice fulfils vow, practice proves faith.
Faith and vows without vigorous practice are hollow faith and floating vows.
The ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school,
Master Ouyi, says:
"This sutra
(the Buddha-Spoken Amitabha Sutra)
takes faith, vows, and name-recitation as the essential purport of practice. Without faith, vows cannot be awakened; without vows, practice cannot be guided;
without the wondrous practice of name-recitation, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized
(The Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra)
The twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, says:

"As for those without faith, let us set them aside for the moment. Even among those who believe: to believe yet not vow is still not to believe. To vow yet not practise is still not to vow. To practise yet not vigorously is still not to practise. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is difficult. If faith is truly genuine, the vow will naturally be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will naturally be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land, surely behold Amitabha, surely realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and surely become a Buddha in one more lifetime."
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)

(Translation: Let those who do not believe in the Pure Land Dharma-gate be set aside for the moment and not spoken of. Even among those who believe in the Pure Land Dharma-gate, to believe yet not vow is like not believing. To vow yet not practise is like not vowing. To practise yet not vigorously is like not practising. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is difficult. If faith is truly genuine, the vow will naturally be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will naturally be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land, surely behold Amitabha, surely realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and surely become a Buddha in one more lifetime.)
And the many fabricators of fallacies about how rebirth may be attained
share one common feature:
they sunder faith and vows from practice. Some even clamour: as long as one has faith and vows, rebirth is attained! Faith itself is rebirth!
The Buddha and the patriarchs teach again and again that one must
recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly,
and again and again they enjoin one to
practise as taught
(see
the Annotation on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha in Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas' Reception
). Therefore one of genuine faith and sincere vows must practise as taught and recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly (see
Single-Minded Recitation, Not Scattered-Mind Recitation
). Those who recite with a scattered mind, precisely because they shrink from hardship and pain, act against the teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs,
which is precisely the concrete expression of faith that is not genuine and vows that are not sincere
(see the teaching of Master Yongming, an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, below). Therefore
those who recite with a scattered mind
are exactly as Master Yongming says:
"their power of faith is faint."
Hence those who recite with a scattered mind surely do not have genuine faith and sincere vows
. The very situation of "scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows" simply does not exist;
it is a false proposition
— just as there is no such thing as a brave soldier who quails on the battlefield.

If one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation can also bring rebirth" means: scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows can also bring rebirth. But since the very situation of "scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows" does not exist at all, how can there be any question of rebirth or no rebirth?
Therefore,
if one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth as well" is utterly fallacious.
Master Yongming
in
the Collection of All Goodness Returning to the One
teaches:
"If words and actions are out of keeping,
and the power of faith is faint,
lacking a mind of unbroken succession of thoughts and having a mind interrupted again and again
(that is, scattered-mind recitation)
Resting in this indolence,
he hopes for rebirth at the moment of death, yet, veiled by his karmic obstacles, he may hardly encounter his good friend, and as wind and fire press upon him,
right mindfulness is not accomplished
[It is feared he may hardly encounter his good friend] It is to be feared that he will hardly meet the great teacher of virtue who can empower him to accomplish right mindfulness at death.
In this passage Master Yongming points out clearly: why is it that people recite with a scattered mind (
"lacking a mind of unbroken succession of thoughts and having a mind interrupted again and again"
)? It is because
their "words and actions are out of keeping and the power of faith is faint."
Therefore one whose words and actions accord, whose faith and vows are genuine and earnest, must be one who recites the Buddha's name single-mindedly.
Scattered-mind recitation, by contrast, shows precisely that such a person is one of
"words and actions out of keeping, and the power of faith faint."
Moreover Master Yongming points out in particular that scattered-mind recitation is a practice of indolence, and if one goes on in this indolence (
"resting in this indolence"
), then at the moment of death
"as wind and fire press upon him, right mindfulness is not accomplished,"
and therefore he does not attain rebirth
[Words and actions out of keeping] Words do not match actions: one says aloud that one has genuine faith and sincere vows, yet one's actual conduct is indolent (neither genuine nor earnest):
"lacking a mind of unbroken succession of thoughts, and having a mind interrupted again and again."
The crux, then, is this: can scattered-mind recitation accomplish right mindfulness at death? For right mindfulness at death is the key to whether one attains rebirth.
On this Master Daochuo teaches:
"The wise diligently gather in the mind; at death the mind is not scattered
(and so they accomplish right mindfulness at death and attain rebirth)
. Those who do not train the mind in single-pointed focus: at death the mind is sure to be scattered
(and so they cannot accomplish right mindfulness at death and revolve in the six realms)
see
Master Daochuo's Pure Land Teaching
) The patriarchs and great masters of every age have all taught and instructed in this way.
Master Yongming therefore goes on to teach:
"Why so? The present life is the cause, death is the fruit; the cause must be made solid, and then the fruit will not be false.
If one would accomplish the ten thoughts at the moment of death
(that is, to accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death)
, then one must make ready the bridge beforehand
that is, to prepare fully in advance
, gather together merit and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, and as long as the thoughts do not fall short
(the succession of thoughts is unbroken)
, then there is nothing to worry about."
(The Collection of All Goodness Returning to the One)
[The ten thoughts at death accomplished] To accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death. (See
Ten Thoughts at Death: Unbroken Succession Brings Rebirth

for the article.) [Making ready the bridge beforehand] One must prepare fully in advance. "Bridge" (jinliang) means a ferry-crossing and a bridge; "to make ready the bridge beforehand" is to prepare fully in advance.

In the teachings above, Master Yongming sets out with perfect clarity the causal relation between faith and vows and practice, and between practice and rebirth: faith and vows are the cause, practice is the fruit; practice is the cause, rebirth is the fruit. Therefore
"the cause must be made solid, and then the fruit will not be false."
The relationship among faith, vows, and practice is this:
faith awakens vow, vow guides practice; practice fulfils vow, practice proves faith.
Question: Master Ouyi says:

"If faith is decisive and the vow is earnest, then even scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth. If faith is not true and the vow is not vigorous, then even one mind undisturbed will not bring rebirth."
(A Treatise on Name-Recitation Passing Through the Nine Grades and Purifying the Four Lands)
Therefore, if one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation can also bring rebirth.
Answer:
"Even scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth"
— this formulation is quite mistaken; Master Ouyi himself corrected it during his lifetime (see
Does Scattered-Mind Recitation Also Surely Bring Rebirth?
). As to why one should advocate single-minded recitation and not scattered-mind recitation,

the reason is this: only through single-minded recitation can the unbroken succession of ten thoughts be accumulated into a habit and made one's nature, so as to ensure the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death, and this is the condition for rebirth
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth
). Scattered-mind recitation means wandering in wild thoughts while reciting; how then could one accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death?
If one cannot accomplish it, one does not attain rebirth — such is the grave consequence of advocating scattered-mind recitation!
Question: Many people, seeing that Master Hanshan says in his Verses on Idle Wasted Effort:
"Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain,"
conclude that scattered-mind recitation cannot bring rebirth. In fact this is quite mistaken. One should know that before these two lines Master Hanshan had already said
"Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a faithful heart is hard; when heart and mouth do not accord, it is always in vain,"

showing that the person who "recites Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered" has heart and mouth at variance and lacks genuine faith and sincere vows. Lacking genuine faith and sincere vows, such a one will of course find rebirth very difficult. Therefore, if one has genuine faith and sincere vows, scattered-mind recitation can also bring rebirth.
Answer: Master Hanshan says:
"Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a faithful heart is hard; when heart and mouth do not accord, it is always in vain."
The "faith" here is not the faith of faith, vows, and practice, but means trustworthiness.
For example, the "xinfeng," or faithful wind, is the wind that, each year, arrives on time as soon as the season comes — a wind that keeps its word.
Master Hanshan's passage therefore:

"Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a faithful heart is hard; when heart and mouth do not accord, it is always in vain. Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain."
means:
reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a heart that is true and trustworthy is hard; when heart and mouth do not accord (
the heart is not true: the mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind dwells on other things
) it is always in vain (all is wasted effort); to recite Amitabha with the mouth while the mind dwells on other things, even though one shouts the throat to bursting, is of no use.
Here Master Hanshan points it out with piercing directness:
"Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered
(scattered-mind recitation)
, though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain."

[Faith] A heart that is true and trustworthy; when heart and mouth do not accord, it is false. Hence the next line is "when heart and mouth do not accord, it is always in vain (all is wasted effort)." The "faith" here is not the faith of faith, vows, and practice, but means trustworthiness. For example, the "xinfeng," or faithful wind, is the wind that, each year, arrives on time as soon as the season comes — a wind that keeps its word. [True and trustworthy] Honest, without deceit. [Though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain] Because "reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered (scattered-mind recitation)" cannot accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death (the most basic requirement for rebirth; see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), one does not attain rebirth and all one's effort is wasted.
A correct theory must be able to stand the test of practice.
Two cases are given here:
1. A case from the Pure Land school.
Master Ouyi also once maintained:
"If faith is decisive and the vow is earnest, then even scattered-mind recitation will surely bring rebirth."
(A Treatise on Name-Recitation Passing Through the Nine Grades and Purifying the Four Lands) More than a month before his passing, the Master wrote
the Vow Text for Founding the Pure Land Society During a Serious Illness
, in which he records how he fared in that illness:
"Now, afflicted by illness,
though my mind is clear, my strength is not my own

, I weep and cry out, not knowing what to do. Fortunately, relying on the Buddha's compassion, my last breath has not yet ceased. If I do not urgently press on in the pure karma, how shall I ever escape the wheel of suffering?"
(Translation:
Now
that illness besets my body, and my heart
within
, al
though
I clearly understand that right mindfulness should be raised and maintained for the sake of rebirth,
yet
my strength is not my own; I weep and cry out,
not knowing what to do
. Fortu
nately
, relying on the Buddha's compas
sion
my life
has not yet ended (if it ended at this moment, the consequences would be unthinkable); if I do not urgently press on in the pure karma
how shall I ever escape the wheel of birth and death?) So the Master wrote the Vow Text for Founding the Pure Land Society During a Serious Illness,
"I invite fellow practitioners of the same aspiration (ten of them), and lay-protector bodhisattva novices (five of them), with minds in harmony, to form a society for three years
(a Pure Land society for three years)
to recite the Buddha's name with diligence, so as to ensure right mindfulness at death and rebirth. (See
the Vow Text for Founding the Pure Land Society During a Serious Illness

[Cry out] To wail and weep aloud. [Right mindfulness] The right mindfulness of the Pure Land school is the thought of reciting the Buddha's name without admixture of wandering thoughts (thought after thought in unbroken succession); the right mindfulness of the Chan school is no-thought (the non-arising of a single thought). [Not knowing what to do] At a loss what to do. Wang means "not"; you means "that which." [Press on (xu)] To strive with effort. [Wheel of suffering] The bitter fruit of birth and death revolves without ceasing, hence it is called a
wheel
2. A case from the Chan school.

Chan Master Keqin (the teacher of Master Dahui) was widely versed in the scriptures and teachings, and took refuge under Wuzu Fayan. One day he entered the master's room to seek instruction, and Keqin reported the state of his cultivation and realization, asking Wuzu for confirmation. However he phrased it, Wuzu said it still would not do. Keqin was unconvinced, and, relying on his wide learning in the scriptures and his eloquence, began to argue boldly with Wuzu. Wuzu, greatly displeased, said:
"Can this withstand birth and death
(can this routine of yours end birth and death)
When the day comes that you sit alone under the solitary lamp in the nirvāṇa hall, test it for yourself
(at the time of death, verify it yourself)
Keqin left in anger. When he reached Jinshan, he fell gravely ill.
In his peril and distress, he applied all that he had learned in his life
(attempting, at this moment of peril, to raise right mindfulness and maintain it)
, and not a single thing was of any use
(Wuzu's prediction was verified)
Recalling Wuzu's words, he then vowed:
"As soon as my illness eases a little
(as soon as I improve even slightly)
, I will return to Wuzu
(turning back from the wrong path)
Later, when he had recovered somewhat, he packed his bundle and returned. Wuzu was delighted at the sight of him (knowing he was material worth shaping), and made him his attendant.

[Chan Master Keqin] Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin Foguo, of the lay surname Luo, was a native of Pengzhou (in present-day Sichuan), whose ancestors had been Confucian scholars for generations. As a child his memory was superb, and he could commit a thousand words to memory each day. ... Chan Master Keqin traveled to various places to study, and finally took refuge under Chan Master Wuzu Fayan. [Wuzu Fayan] Chan Master Fayan of Mount Wuzu. [Nirvāṇa hall] The place where sick monks are sent to enter extinction.
The two cases above were tested at the point of mortal illness. In his mortal illness Master Ouyi discovered the grave problem that "
though my mind is clear, my strength is not my own"

and at once repented before the Buddha and founded the Pure Land Society, reciting the Buddha's name with diligence, with diligence in single-minded recitation, of course. And in his mortal illness Chan Master Keqin discovered the grave problem that
"when he applied all that he had learned in his life, not a single thing was of any use"
and at once vowed that as soon as his illness eased he would return to Wuzu and practise according to his guidance.
[Though my mind is clear, my strength is not my own] More than three hundred years have passed, and even now there are people loudly advocating scattered-mind recitation! May I ask:
can scattered-mind recitation make one's strength one's own?
The patriarch of the Pure Land school nearest to our own time,
Master Yinguang, like the patriarchs of every generation of the Pure Land school (see
Does Scattered-Mind Recitation Also Surely Bring Rebirth?
), earnestly and repeatedly taught single-minded recitation (recitation with the mind gathered in). Master Yinguang teaches:
"Recitation with the mind gathered in
is the settled and unchanging path
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
First Letter in Reply to the Layman Liu Guanshan)
Because scattered-mind recitation can hardly attain rebirth.
Single-minded recitation surely attains rebirth.
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Letter to the Layman Chen Xizhou)
"If the six faculties are not gathered in, then even though one recites the Buddha's name, the mind still teems with wandering thoughts,
and one hardly gains the real benefit
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Letter in Reply to Master Huanxiu)

Why do you stop your ears to all this? [Recitation with the mind gathered in] To gather in the mind is to focus it on a single object, free from scatteredness and torpor. Therefore recitation with the mind gathered in is single-minded recitation.

In fact, you need not wait for mortal illness to test this; you can test right now whether scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth. The most basic requirement for rebirth is the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death. Take up scattered-mind recitation, and see whether you can accomplish that unbroken succession of ten thoughts. Further, can you accumulate it into a habit and make it your nature? If you can, then scattered-mind recitation can also bring rebirth; if you cannot, then scattered-mind recitation cannot bring rebirth.

Analyse it more carefully still: to accumulate the unbroken succession of ten thoughts into a habit and make it one's nature, one must recite the Buddha's name in an unbroken succession of ten thoughts at all times and in all places; and to recite in that way is single-minded recitation, not scattered-mind recitation.
From this we know that scattered-mind recitation cannot bring rebirth.
This is why Master Hanshan says:
"Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered
(scattered-mind recitation)
, though you shout the throat to bursting, it is all in vain."
(Verses on Idle Wasted Effort; for the annotation see
Annotated Verses on Idle Wasted Effort

Here I set forth the instructions on how to practise Buddha-recitation given by Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both incarnations of Amitabha Buddha. Those who advocate reciting with a scattered mind may hold up their own words and actions for comparison and see how they are deceiving sentient beings.
Master Shandao taught:
With a single-pointed mind
recite solely the name of Amitabha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration, never abandoning it thought after thought
(an unbroken succession of thoughts)
— such a one is named the karma of right concentration,
in accord with that Buddha's
(Amitabha Buddha's)
vow
Unbroken succession brings rebirth.
If one can keep
thought after thought unbroken until the very end of life,
then ten of ten are reborn and a hundred of a hundred.
May all people reflect on this well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the will and master oneself
(spurring oneself on and holding oneself in check),
never letting the effort flag by day or night;
when the previous thought comes to an end,
the next thought is immediately born.
To forever relish the unconditioned joy of the Dharma, even up to the attainment of Buddhahood — how wondrous a thing it is!
Master Yongming taught:
If words and actions are out of keeping,
and the power of faith is faint,
one who lacks
a mind of unbroken succession of thoughts
but rather a mind interrupted again and again
(the thought of recitation is cut off again and again by wandering thoughts — this is scattered-mind recitation),
and
resting in this indolence,
hopes for rebirth at the moment of death, yet, veiled by his karma, may hardly encounter his good spiritual friend
(it is feared he will not meet the great teacher of virtue who can sustain his right mindfulness at death),
and as the wind and fire press on him,
right mindfulness is not accomplished
Why so?
The present life is the cause, death is the fruit;
the cause must be made solid, and then the fruit will not be false. If one would bring about
the ten thoughts at the moment of death,
(that is, to accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death),
then one must
make ready the bridge beforehand
(that is, to prepare fully in advance),
gather together merit and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death),
and as long as the thoughts do not fall short
(i.e., the succession of thoughts is unbroken),
then there is nothing to worry about.
Question: An article says: “Master Shandao, in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, says: ‘
From the contemplation of the sun down through the thirteenth contemplation is called concentrated good; the three kinds of merit and the nine grades are called scattered good.’
The three kinds of merit and even the nine grades
— even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade is scattered good.
Thus we know that
if you have genuine faith and a sincere vow, scattered-mind recitation will absolutely, one hundred percent, lead to rebirth.
” Is this so?

Answer: The logic of that passage is: “The three kinds of merit and even the nine grades — even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade — are scattered good”; scattered-mind recitation is scattered good, and so “scattered-mind recitation will absolutely one hundred percent lead to rebirth.” If we follow this logic, then since “even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade is scattered good,” that highest rebirth likewise is all through scattered-mind recitation! This is a complete distortion of “scattered good” in the Contemplation Sutra. The “scattered” of scattered good is spoken in contrast to the “concentrated” of the sustained, focused, and subtle contemplation-aim of the first thirteen contemplations (see
the Annotation on the Lowest-Grade Lowest-Birth Chapter of the Contemplation Sutra
) that is sustained and single-minded toward a subtle object of contemplation. Whereas the “scattered” of scattered-mind recitation means that one wanders in wild thoughts while reciting. Therefore,
these two “scattered” do not carry the same meaning

In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao also lays great stress on single-minded recitation. If scattered-mind recitation were scattered good, why would Master Shandao in that very same writing still teach that “
single-minded recitation is the true proper practice
”? Master Shandao says:

“Practice, however, is of two kinds: the first is proper practice, and the second is mixed practice. As for proper practice, one who relies solely upon the practices given in the rebirth sutras is called a practitioner of proper practice. What does that mean?
With a single mind,
single-heartedly read and recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Immeasurable Life Sutra, and the like;
with single-minded focus
contemplate, observe, and recollect the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If one bows, then
with a single mind
single-heartedly bow to that Buddha; if one recites aloud, then
with a single mind single-heartedly call upon that Buddha
; if one praises and offers, then with a single mind single-heartedly praise and offer.
This is called proper practice
With a single mind, single-heartedly recollect the name of Amitabha Buddha
, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration,
the one who never abandons it thought after thought
(never interrupted by wandering thoughts)
— this is named
the karma of right concentration
(For the commentary see
the Pure Land Teachings of Master Shandao
.) If scattered-mind recitation were scattered good, why would Master Shandao, in that same book, still treat single-minded recitation as a special topic, and even hold it up as
the karma of right concentration
! Therefore,

Master Shandao's instructions on scattered good and his instructions on single-minded recitation in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra together prove that scattered-mind recitation is not scattered good, because scattered-mind recitation is not proper practice; single-minded recitation is the proper practice!
Master Shandao says:

“Practice, however, is of two kinds: the first is proper practice, and the second is mixed practice. As for proper practice, one who relies solely upon the practices given in the rebirth sutras is called a practitioner of proper practice. What does that mean?
If one recites aloud, then
with a single mind single-heartedly call upon that Buddha
this is called the proper practice

In fact, “if you have genuine faith and a sincere vow, scattered-mind recitation will absolutely one hundred percent lead to rebirth” is utterly fallacious. Where is there anyone of genuine faith and sincere vow who still recites with a scattered mind? Those who recite with a scattered mind do so precisely because they shrink from hardship and pain, and therefore act against the instruction of the Buddha and the patriarchs — this is precisely the concrete expression of faith that is not genuine and vows that are not sincere. Therefore, those who recite with a scattered mind surely do not have genuine faith and sincere vows. The very situation of “scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows” simply does not exist; it is a false proposition, just as there is no such thing as a brave soldier who quails on the battlefield. (See the discussion above.)

Question: An article says: “Venerable Miaolian, who passed away a few years ago and who, in twenty years, practised the Pratyutpanna Samādhi ten times, made his forty-ninth great vow: that even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth.” Is this so?

Answer: As far as I know, Venerable Miaolian's forty-ninth great vow was: “Whoever has seen my face, heard my teaching, or even heard my name, I shall deliver them all to be reborn together in the Western Pure Land; if in this life they fail to be reborn there, I shall surely return again to teach and deliver them, until they are reborn in the West.” It was not: “Even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth.” You may go online and verify.

If someone truly makes a forty-ninth great vow of “even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth,” then he is slandering the Buddha and is accusing Amitabha Buddha of not coming to fetch the beings who recite with a scattered mind. Such a person, who does not understand the Dharma himself, yet so arrogantly makes such a forty-ninth great vow, wishing to rise above Amitabha Buddha, the King among Buddhas!
[King among Buddhas] The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitabha Buddha says:

“Amitabha Buddha's light is pure and free from stain, without flaw or diminution. The light of Amitabha Buddha is lovely and surpasses the brightness of the sun and moon by a hundred thousand millions of times. It is the brightest among all Buddhas' lights, the finest among lights, the most majestic among lights, the most swift and good among lights,
the King among all Buddhas,
the most honoured of lights, the brightest and most immeasurable of lights.”
In fact,
at the moment of the death of every single being, Amitabha Buddha is there to welcome him,
including those who have recited with a scattered mind.
It is only that beings without right mindfulness at the point of death cannot see it, and so they follow their own wandering thoughts and are reborn according to their karma.
Therefore, one must hold right mindfulness at death before he can see Amitabha Buddha come to welcome him and, following the Buddha, be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honoured as the ancient Buddha of Jiangnan, taught in the “Three Sessions of Remembrance”:
Although it is said that Amitabha gathers in beings for their rebirth, one must believe
it is only one's own mind that manifests it,
that is,
the mutual resonance of the mind and the Buddha,
and that in the end
(after all)
it is not obtained from outside

[Only the self-manifestation of one's own mind] Amitabha Buddha's coming to welcome (gather in) beings is solely the manifestation of one's own mind; this is because of the mutual resonance of sympathetic response, and is not something obtained from outside. Therefore only those with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while the others around them cannot. Those beings who are deluded at death, because their minds are turbid and confused and they lack the sense of right mindfulness (the unbroken succession of ten thoughts), naturally will not have Amitabha Buddha's coming to welcome them appear in their minds, and so they cannot see the Buddha come —
not because Amitabha Buddha did not come to welcome them
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha says:
“That land does not turn anyone away
(the Pure Land refuses no being rebirth there)
but is drawn along by nature
(those beings who do not attain rebirth in the Pure Land naturally follow their own dying wandering thoughts and are born into the six realms)
Therefore, rebirth or not depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death)
This is why
Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both avatars of Amitabha Buddha, earnestly teach again and again:
one must accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death
(see
the Eighteenth Vow
article)
. This, after all, is the instruction of Amitabha Buddha himself!
[Mutual resonance of sympathetic response] The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha interpenetrate each other.
[Those beings who do not attain rebirth in the Pure Land naturally follow their dying wandering thoughts and are reborn in the six realms] On this matter, Master Lianchi taught:
Those who are deluded at death

, because all their lives they indulged their wandering thoughts, never cultivating right mindfulness, and their minds were mostly scattered and confused. At the time when the warmth of the body is about to leave
(the moment when the four elements break apart)

, the deeds of a whole life all appear before them, and their minds tremble with terror and their movements become frantic. The one who should descend to hell sees the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a garden. The one who should fall among the animals takes the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a hall. Even those who have done good and should be reborn among humans or gods cannot escape loving and hating their parents. Even the lesser sages of the lesser vehicle and those newly resolved on the mind of enlightenment cannot know rightly their coming in and going out. All of these are what is called delusion. Riding on this delusion, they are born according to karma within the three realms and the seven destinies. ...... As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ Again he said: ‘All lands are held by thought alone.’ When pure thought is accomplished, rebirth is surely obtained; of this there is no doubt at all.”

(The Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra) Modern rendering: Those who are deluded at death are all those who all their lives went along with their wandering thoughts, never cultivating right mindfulness, and their minds were mostly scattered and confused. When the four elements break apart, the deeds of a whole life all appear before them, and their minds tremble with terror and their movements all go amiss. The one who should descend to hell takes the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a beautiful garden. The one who should fall among the animals takes the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a splendid hall. Even those who do good and should be reborn among humans or gods cannot, when entering the womb, escape loving the mother and hating the father so as to be born a man, or loving the father and hating the mother so as to be born a woman. Even the first fruit of the lesser vehicle and the bodhisattvas who have just begun their resolve still have the delusion of the intermediate life between births, and cannot know rightly their entering and leaving the womb. All of these are delusion. Because of this delusion at death, they are born according to karma within the seven destinies of the three realms. ...... As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ (When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is also pure.) The Buddha also said: ‘All lands are held by thought alone.’ (All lands are wholly upheld by the thought of the mind.) Therefore, when the pure thought of a recitation-practitioner is accomplished, rebirth in the Western Pure Land is surely obtained. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt. [Seven destinies] Hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, spirits, heavens, and asuras. “Destiny” means that toward which one goes. [Buddha-land] The domain that a single Buddha teaches and transforms; there are pure lands, impure lands, reward lands, and dharmakāya lands.

On the principle of the mutual resonance of sympathetic response at the moment of death, Master Yinguang, the incarnation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, taught in the Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners:

The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vows and, with utmost sincerity, call upon the Buddha, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and not utterly sincere, but accords with greed, anger, and ignorance and turns its back on the Buddha, it is like water that is turbid and restless; the moon, though it does not fail to shine upon it, still cannot be clearly imaged in it.”

Rendering: The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vows and call upon the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (the metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness calling forth Amitabha Buddha's welcome). If the mind is not pure, not utterly sincere, in accord with greed, anger, and ignorance, and opposed to the Buddha, it is like water that is turbid and restless; the Buddha-moon, though it does not fail to shine upon it (the metaphor that Amitabha Buddha is always coming to welcome every being at death), still cannot be clearly imaged there (the metaphor that a restless, turbid mind cannot present the Buddha's welcome, but follows its own wandering thoughts and is reborn according to karma).

Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is turbid and in motion it is hidden. The moon is surely without preference or rejection; that it does not appear is simply because the water is murky and surging and has no way to take in its reflection.”

Rendering: Only when the water is clear and still does the image of the moon appear; when the water is turbid and in motion, the moon's image does not appear. The moon indeed shines without choosing or rejecting; the reason it does not appear is that the water is murky and surging, so that it cannot bring forth the moon's reflection. (The metaphor: only those beings with right mindfulness at death can see Amitabha Buddha's welcome, while beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see it. Amitabha Buddha indeed welcomes every being at death without choosing or rejecting; the reason those without right mindfulness cannot see him is that their own minds are murky, turbid, and scattered, so they follow their wandering thoughts and are reborn according to their karma.)

Therefore, for the recitation-practitioner, single-minded right mindfulness at death is of utmost importance. A thousand thoughts, ten thousand thoughts, even thinking throughout the whole day and the whole year, is for nothing other than to make ripe this one thought of recitation,
so as to ensure that at the moment of death this thought continues without interruption and calls forth Amitabha Buddha's welcome
. Therefore, Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both avatars of Amitabha Buddha, earnestly teach again and again:
one must accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death
(see
the Conditions for Rebirth
This is the word of the sage! If one will not listen to the words of Amitabha Buddha, whose words will he listen to?

[Succession] The thought of recitation following one upon another, unmixed with wandering thoughts. [The measure of the sage's word] This is spoken by the sage, correct and without error, and is certainly to be believed and received.
